items.title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
items.original_title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
items.summary: Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. According to the Jordan Shipping Association, Aqaba handled 37,182 Iraq-bound transit containers during the first seven months of 2026, compared with just 3,599 during the corresponding period last year, a 933% increase. Hapag-Lloyd outlined a routing in July whereby containers are discharged at Khorfakkan, outside the Strait of Hormuz, before being trucked across the UAE to Sharjah or Jebel Ali and transferred onto third-party feeder vessels serving Iraq and other upper Gulf destinations.

items.title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.original_title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.summary: Ports and terminals are no strangers to reinvention. Over the past 50 years, the industry has managed and adapted to the shift to containerization and ever-larger vessels, the move from paper manifests to electronic messaging and transactions, and the subsequent evolution to system-to-system integration with other parties in the shipping industries. But many port functions still run on clipboards, radio calls, or the gut instincts of a planner, who has watched the yard fill up and empty thousands of times. To assess how far the industry has come, BCG and TIC4.0 (an international nonprofit association of terminal operators and equipment and solution providers dedicated to the creation and promotion of digital standards for the cargo-handling industry) surveyed more than 100 leaders from across the container ports and terminals ecosystem. On average, those we surveyed are already using or exploring the top 16 of the 43 use cases we assessed, from extracting data from shipping documents (62%) to predicting when a crane or straddle carrier will fail (48%). Survey Demographics In August 2026, BCG and the Terminal Industry Committee 4.0 (TIC4.0) surveyed the port and terminal ecosystem on the adoption of AI and generative AI, to establish where the industry sees the opportunity and where it sees the risk.

items.original_title: MPA and China Classification Society Strengthen Partnership for a Greener, Smarter Maritime Future
items.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and the China Classification Society (CCS) have renewed their Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to strengthen collaboration in maritime decarbonisation, digitalisation and talent development in Singapore. The MOU was renewed during the Sixth North Bund International Shipping Forum in Shanghai, building on the partnership established in 2023. Since 2023, MPA and CCS have worked with local research and industry partners on projects ranging from the use of B100 biofuel on harbour craft to the evaluation, testing and verification for smart ships. Under the renewed agreement, MPA and CCS will expand their collaboration on research and development in decarbonisation, including green fuel value chain, marine electrification and energy efficiency technologies for vessels. Both organisations will also deepen collaboration on digital and smart ship initiatives, such as digital testing and risk assessment for autonomous vessels, to support research and innovation in the maritime sector. Both organisations will also collaborate to support talent development through programmes such as the MPA Global Internship Awards, the MaritimeONE Scholarship Programme and internships, as well as attachments which will provide students and aspiring maritime professionals with exposure to international maritime companies and industry practices.

items.title: ESI 2.0 prompts ports to rethink environmental incentive schemes
items.original_title: ESI 2.0 prompts ports to rethink environmental incentive schemes
items.summary: The updated Environmental Ship Index (ESI 2.0) is prompting ports to review how they reward better environmental performance, as the new methodology brings vessel scoring more closely in line with the environmental priorities shaping shipping today. Developed and owned by IAPH and administered globally by OceanScore, ESI provides ports with a framework for identifying and incentivising vessels that perform beyond environmental standards. ESI 2.0 updates this framework to reflect developments in regulation, technology and vessel operations, with increased recognition of areas including energy use, greenhouse gas performance, innovation and electrification. ESI 2.0 reflects the priorities of shipping today As shipping adopts cleaner fuels, electrification and new emissions-reduction technologies, the way environmental performance is measured also needs to evolve. Port of Aarhus turns the new methodology into action To understand the impact of ESI 2.0, OceanScore analysed Port of Aarhus’ 2025 vessel calls and how its existing incentive scheme would perform under the updated methodology. Keeping incentives effective as shipping evolves The Aarhus example demonstrates how ports can respond to changes in environmental performance measurement while keeping their incentive schemes relevant to the vessels they serve. “ESI 2.0 reflects how environmental priorities in shipping are evolving, and the Aarhus example shows how ports can translate that into practical incentives,” says Thomas Smith, Head of Cargo Solutions at OceanScore.

Together with the vessel studies and technical validation, these activities will provide a broader basis for assessing the integration, safety, environmental performance and economic implications of the complete MARPOWER system. items.title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.original_title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.summary: Shipping’s drive to digitalise risks slowing itself down as fragmented software, weak digital training and growing pressure to adopt artificial intelligence add complexity to operational and commercial decisions, according to OrbitMI. OrbitMI warns that the sector is entering a period of ‘digital fatigue’: growing scepticism and frustration when technology fails to deliver the promised simplicity or measurable productivity and performance improvement gains. After years of adding platforms and bolt-on applications, many teams still transfer data manually, work across separate dashboards and adapt established processes to generic interfaces. Research by Thetius and Marcura found that 82% of maritime professionals believe AI can improve efficiency and 81% are running pilots, but only 11% have the policies and governance needed to scale it. Two-thirds are concerned that overreliance on AI could erode human judgement, while 69% worry it may miss critical red flags in contracts or voyage planning. What users need are tools that are truly collaborative and are fully integrated in their workflows; always present but never intrusive. OrbitMI has been investing in this approach through the acquisition of AI specialist AuQub and maritime advisory and voyage optimisation business Gale Force, alongside the expansion of its maritime, product and technology leadership over the past 18 months.

items.title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.original_title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports.

South Korean oil tankers had originally, from April, loaded crude at Yanbu Port on the Red Sea and entered South Korea via the southern Bab el-Mandeb Strait. As the closure of the Strait of Hormuz becomes prolonged, detour shipments to secure domestic energy supply are expected to continue for the time being. So far, a total of 19 South Korean vessels have transported crude oil through the Red Sea. SPOT © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS/Handout via REUTERS Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify ships operating without reliable Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. The agreement, announced Tuesday , will integrate imagery from Airbus’s SPOT Earth observation satellites with Kpler’s existing vessel-tracking network, allowing analysts to detect ships independently of their reported AIS positions. The service will use high-resolution satellite imagery, with a resolution of 1.5 meters and a 60-kilometer swath, combined with artificial intelligence to identify vessels at sea and in port. The technology is intended to address a growing challenge for maritime tracking: determining whether a vessel has deliberately switched off or manipulated its AIS signal, or whether its reported position has been affected by interference with satellite navigation systems. By comparing AIS data with independently captured satellite imagery, Kpler says it can better distinguish between the two. items.title: Supply Constraints Keep Asian Coal Prices High
items.original_title: Supply Constraints Keep Asian Coal Prices High
items.summary: Asian thermal coal prices are likely to stay elevated in the near term as Indonesian supply uncertainty and lower Chinese production limit supply, says Fitch Ratings. Demand from gas-to-coal switching in Japan and Korea is likely to stay firm, driven by the Middle East conflict, pushing regional prices higher – particularly for high- Calorific Value (CV) coal. Firmer prices will support miners’ near-term cash flow and debt-servicing capacity, but not reverse longer-term pressure from declining Chinese and Indian import requirements and the energy transition. Indonesian export supply is likely to remain difficult to predict despite the government easing its (initially) much lower 2026 production coal output target of 600 million tonnes (2025: actual output 790 million). Chinese coal supply should recover as tighter safety inspections following May’s Shanxi mine accident ease gradually. Chinese demand, which accounted for over one-third of Asian seaborne thermal-coal imports in 2025, should provide limited support once domestic production normalises. High gas prices should have limited implications for Chinese coal demand because gas-fired generation accounts for only a small share of the power mix. S&SEA coal demand remains robust, supported by 5%-7% power demand growth, weaker hydropower output, and transmission constraints on renewable additions. Qinhuangdao 5,500 kcal/kg thermal coal exceeded CNY1,000/tonne in early October despite seasonally weak demand.

items.title: Eastern Pacific links wind propulsion repayments to fuel savings
items.original_title: Eastern Pacific links wind propulsion repayments to fuel savings
items.summary: Singapore-based Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has secured financing for wind-assisted propulsion systems on two vessels through a fund linking repayments to independently verified fuel savings. The Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET), managed by AIM Horizon Investments with the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) as decarbonisation adviser, is making its first deployment with the EPS projects. The vessels, Pacific Sentinel and Pacific Sunstone , have each been fitted with three 22-metre suction sails, making them the first ships in the EPS fleet to adopt wind-assisted propulsion. FEET offers up to 100% upfront financing for energy efficiency technologies, with shipowners making payments based on verified fuel and regulatory savings. The financing model builds on earlier trials involving GCMD and EPS aboard Pacific Sentinel , during which researchers collected 276m data points over four months of trading in the Americas between May and September 2025. The analysis examined 203 valid sail on-off transitions to isolate the technology’s impact on fuel consumption from changing operating conditions. The methodology has undergone independent review, with future project savings subject to verification before payments are calculated. “Decarbonisation moves faster when the technology, the data, and the financing come together,” said EPS chief executive Cyril Ducau.

items.title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.original_title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.summary: In an industry where a position list is a competitive weapon, the question is no longer just how to comply—but where carbon decisions are made and who controls the data behind them, said Argyris Zafeiropoulos, principal advisor at Resilience & Compliance Advisory. With the EU Emissions Trading System fully phased into shipping and FuelEU Maritime tightening year by year, carbon is now a line item in every fixture. On a single laden Aframax voyage from the Gulf to Rotterdam, the FuelEU penalty alone climbs to about €246,000 ($276,000) by 2040 — same ship, same route, same fuel. Far less attention goes to a quieter question: where are these carbon decisions actually made, and who can see the data behind them? On that voyage, ETS and FuelEU together come to about €104,000 ($116,600) at an €81 ($91) allowance price — roughly one euro ($1.12) on every tonne of a 100,000-tonne cargo, rising to about €1.36 ($1.53) by 2030. In commodity trades, the choice between CIF and FOB helps decide who absorbs it. Carbon has moved beyond the charter party and into the commodity contract. Shipping has always rewarded those who control their critical assets — ships, cargo relationships, market intelligence and commercial judgement.

items.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway. Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil. The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. “An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room,” Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying. The tanker was travelling in the strait’s “unauthorized southern route” and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said. It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines. The Guards’ naval commander Admiral Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile.” The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports in response to Tehran’s blockade on the waterway. Maersk said the new service was designed to complement its other Asia-Europe strings as well as flows from Asia to West Africa and South America with its west Mediterranean hubs taking on more relay transhipment responsibilities. As a result, Gemini’s Asia-North Europe Loop 1 (Maersk AE2/Hapag NE1) will replace its current first European port of call of Tangier with Rotterdam, “providing an alternative and improved service from Ningbo and Shanghai to Rotterdam”.

Shipping the order directly from outside the EU would incur €6 in customs duty and an expected €4 handling fee. Adding assumed postage and clearance costs of €7, plus €2.50 for storage, picking and packing, produces a total of €19.50. Holdwise calculated €2 in normal customs duty, 50 cents per order for allocated freight and clearance, €2.50 for warehouse fulfilment and €5 for delivery within the EU: a total of €10.

items.original_title: India rolls out credit risk backstop for shipbuilders
items.summary: India has introduced two government-backed credit-risk insurance products for shipbuilders, aiming to protect domestic yards against missed payments and buyer defaults on vessel construction contracts. The measures, unveiled by shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal, form part of New Delhi’s wider shipbuilding development programme, which has earmarked INR14.43bn ($152m) for credit-risk coverage. The first product, Shipbuilding Project Credit Risk Insurance Policy, has been developed by state-owned export credit insurer ECGC and will cover shipbuilding contracts for overseas owners. The second, Business Credit Shield Policy–Shipbuilders, has been developed by New India Assurance and targets domestic shipbuilding projects. The initiative addresses one of the financial risks facing shipbuilders, particularly on large contracts where construction can take several years and payments are tied to milestones. Delayed instalments or buyer defaults can leave yards exposed to substantial working capital requirements while vessels remain under construction. The two products were introduced under India’s $2.1bn shipbuilding development scheme, part of a wider maritime investment package approved by the government in September 2025. The roughly $152m allocation is part of that existing programme. India has been stepping up financial support for its shipbuilding industry as it seeks to expand domestic construction capacity and attract more international orders.

A study published by European Community Shipowners’ Associations (ECSA) estimates that the proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism needs at least 330m allowances, compared with the 110m currently envisaged by the European Commission. The association puts the required support at around €30bn ($33.6bn), aimed at narrowing the cost gap between conventional marine fuels and cleaner alternatives. The proposal forms part of the ongoing revision of the EU ETS and remains subject to approval by the European Parliament and Council. With the phase-in period completed, shipping companies must surrender allowances covering 100% of their emissions falling within the ETS framework from the 2026 emissions year. The association estimates that shipowners purchase roughly 90m allowances annually. At an illustrative carbon price of €100 per allowance, that would represent an annual outlay of approximately €9bn ($10.1bn). ECSA argues that the proposed reserve, covering 2028 to 2040, would meet only about one-third of the industry’s estimated requirements. The intervention comes as shipowners weigh increasing carbon compliance costs against the substantial premiums associated with alternative fuels, fleet upgrades and new propulsion systems.

items.title: Asia-US container rates mixed as extended peak season demand wanes; tanker rates stable

items.summary: Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were mixed this week while rates for liquid chemical tankers ex-US Gulf were largely stable. Rates to the West Coast are between $7,475-8,300/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast are between $9,600-11,300/FEU, remaining near the highest since mid-2022 for both routes. Rates from supply chain advisors Drewry rose by 3% from Shanghai to Los Angeles while rates from Shanghai to New York fell by 1%, as shown in the following chart. Drewry said it expects rates to be less volatile next week as capacity is expected to be stable amid management via blank sailings. Judah Levine, head of research at Freightos, said rates have been supported at current levels by sustained peak season demand together with congestion at Asian ports. The National Retail Foundation (NRF) projects November arrivals to drop 11% month on month, suggesting that peak season is finally coming to an end and that rates may ease until demand pressure from the pre-Lunar New Year rush kicks in late this year or starting in January. Rates from the USG to ARA trade lane remain unchanged; however, demand along this route continues to be slow following EPCA, leading to further downward pressure on rates, despite somewhat limited open available space.

items.title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.original_title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.summary: Look at it from the viewpoint of a shipper moving goods by containership on the Asia-Europe route. The proportion of ships on this route which arrived on the scheduled day of arrival declined from 51% in May to just 31% in September (average of all ports and all carriers), according to the Drewry Container Capacity Insight. Even the Gemini alliance, which has a higher-than-average track record for on-time arrivals, managed just 34% in September. The Asia-Europe trade’s schedule reliability scores by carrier in September ranged between 19% and 38% and the proportion of sailings not cancelled ranged between 0% and 23%, according to Drewry’s analysis for this route. Looking at this from a carrier viewpoint, the logic is that cargo volumes were strong in the peak season, port congestion got worse in Asia, but the carriers could make higher profits by throwing more ship capacity at the market and cancelling fewer sailings… which must have made port congestion worse. At Drewry, we are looking more closely at how carrier performance, port congestion and network exposure can be brought together to give shippers a clearer picture of where they may be vulnerable. Ultimately, the aim should be to move away from simply reacting to delays and towards building those risks into carrier selection, procurement strategies and contingency planning.
